title: user-api flapping in and out of the load balancer
intro: Customers report intermittent 502s hitting user-api, but the pods all show as Running. Nothing looks obviously broken at first glance.

steps.prompt: Check the pods — confirm they really are all Running.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
user-api-6b8d9f7c4-a1b2c    0/1     Running   0          2h
user-api-6b8d9f7c4-d3e4f    1/1     Running   0          2h
user-api-6b8d9f7c4-g5h6i    0/1     Running   0          2h
steps.hint: Look closely at the READY column, not just STATUS.

steps.prompt: Two of three pods show READY 0/1 despite Running. Check the endpoints behind the user-api service — are those two even receiving traffic?
steps.hint: Only READY pods get added to a Service's endpoints — compare this list against the pod count.

steps.prompt: Only one pod's IP is in the endpoint list, confirming 2 of 3 are being skipped. Describe one of the not-ready pods to see why.
steps.fake_output:
Readiness: http-get http://:8080/ready delay=0s timeout=1s period=5s #success=1 #failure=1
Events:
  Warning  Unhealthy  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
steps.hint: The readiness probe itself is what's failing — that's a strong lead.

steps.prompt: The probe fails intermittently with 503, not always. Check the pod's logs around the same time.
steps.fake_output:
10:14:58 GET /ready 200
10:15:03 GET /ready 503 - db connection pool exhausted
10:15:08 GET /ready 200
steps.hint: The app's own logs will show what /ready is actually checking when it fails.

steps.prompt: The readiness check queries the database connection pool, and it's intermittently exhausted under load. Check how many replicas are actually configured versus available.
steps.fake_output:
NAME       READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
user-api   1/3     3            1          2h
steps.hint: Compare desired vs available — this tells you if the deployment is simply under-provisioned for current load.

resolution: user-api's /ready endpoint checks its database connection pool as part of readiness, which is reasonable — but the pool size is too small for current traffic, so under load it intermittently reports itself unready, gets pulled from the Service's endpoints, and the remaining pods absorb even more load, making it worse (a self-reinforcing spiral). Two real fixes are needed: raise the connection pool size per pod, and scale up user-api's replica count so no single pod carries this much load. Restarting pods would NOT have fixed this — the pods were never actually broken, they were correctly reporting real backend pressure.
